children.value: Countries are grouped into tiers by the IO data available for them, from the most detailed and annually updated (Tier 0) to countries with no usable published table (Tier 3).
The model covers 148 countries plus a rest-of-world region. A country’s tier sets which type of table it starts from, how much sector detail that table has, and how it is valued.

The U.S. starts from Make and Use tables for 2024 that Cornerstone produces each year (nowcast tables). They follow the schema of the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) 2017 detailed tables, after redefinitions. BEA’s own detailed tables come out only every five years, and the latest are for 2017; our tables estimate the 2024 economy in the same form. The Make table shows which commodities each industry produces. The Use table shows which commodities each industry and each final user buys. Both are in millions of dollars.

Many establishments make secondary products. A hotel runs a restaurant, for example, or a manufacturer does its own repair work. Redefinitions move these secondary products, and the inputs used to make them, to the industry where they are the primary product. Each industry’s input recipe then describes the product it is named for more closely, which makes for cleaner emission factors.

Most of the remaining large economies come from one of two multi-regional tables, FIGARO or ICIO. Both are already harmonized across countries, but they are much coarser than the U.S. tables. Where a country is in both, we use FIGARO.

Both are inter-country tables, so each country’s own block of the table gives its domestic inputs, and the blocks for all other countries give its imports.

Before mapping, five of FIGARO’s broad sectors are split into finer ones while keeping their totals: electricity, gas, and heat; water, sewerage, and waste; basic metals (steel, other ferrous, non-ferrous); non-metallic minerals (cement, other); mining (five sectors); and agriculture (11 farm sectors). The 83 countries that are in neither Tier 1 nor Tier 2 have no usable published table. They are not part of the multi-region table; their factors are calculated one country at a time.
All 83 share one template recipe, a weighted blend of three Tier 2 economies: Mexico (30%), Malaysia (30%), and Tunisia (40%).
Each country’s own import share splits the template into domestic and imported inputs, with the same share for every sector. The supply chains behind those imports are approximated with China’s.
Direct emission intensities are scaled to the country’s own emissions per unit of GDP, and electricity uses the country’s own emission intensity.

Decision for the team, Tier 3 vs. rest of world: imports from Tier 3 countries get the rest-of-world proxy (Colombia, Mexico, Türkiye, Chile), while those countries’ own factors use the Tier 3 template (Mexico, Malaysia, Tunisia) with country-specific emission intensities. Either give the rest-of-world region intensities based on the Tier 3 countries, or keep the proxy as documented in the IO overview’s assumptions.

🖼 Share of global output and emissions by tier

Tier 3 countries share one template input recipe. Each country differs only in its overall import share, applied equally to every sector, and in its direct emission intensities, which are scaled to the country’s emissions per unit of GDP, with its own electricity intensity. Their imported supply chains are approximated with China’s.
These countries have no usable published IO table.

Differences in industry structure between Tier 3 countries are not captured, and imports from countries other than China are given China’s supply chains. Factors for these countries carry more uncertainty than those for Tiers 0 to 2.
